strengths: The SLR framework is well-motivated: fully automated synthesis of ILP tasks with deterministic, executable symbolic evaluation removes LLM-judge noise and annotation cost, and the paper provides a clear algorithmic description (Alg. 1) of rule synthesis, stratified background sampling, and reward computation.

SLR-BENCH is a substantial and useful artifact: 19k tasks across a 20-level curriculum with precisely controlled difficulty (rule length, problem size, vocabulary, sampling policy), and the claimed combinatorial space is large, mitigating memorization concerns.

The large-scale evaluation of ~16 conventional and reasoning LLMs yields genuinely interesting findings: high syntactic validity but low logical accuracy, sharp performance collapse with complexity, diminishing returns from test-time compute, and cost analysis (e.g., $300/1k prompts for o3) that is timely and rarely reported.

The curriculum-learning result (roughly doubling Llama-3.1-8B accuracy on SLR-BENCH with gains on MMLU subsets, LogiQA, GPQA, ARC, HellaSwag) is a valuable demonstration that synthetic logic curricula can transfer downstream, and training/evaluation details (App. G) are sufficiently concrete to support reproduction.

Comprehensive appendix (task specification, grounding domains, LLM-guided rule generation prompts, pricing), honest limitations section, and a stated commitment to releasing code and data under permissive licenses.
weaknesses: Narrow task scope relative to the framing: SLR-BENCH instantiates only the Michalski trains domain with single-target, function-free definite clauses; the headline claim that 'LLMs can't do induction at scale' is supported only within this restricted ILP family, and generalization to broader inductive reasoning is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The evaluation conflates hypothesis search with logical correctness: because the symbolic judge scores only separation of E+ and E-, any perfectly separating hypothesis counts as 'solved' (or the prompt asks for the shortest rule, whose uniqueness is not verified); with multiple models the paper does not clearly disentangle recovery of the ground-truth rule R* from mere example separation, weakening claims about 'correct logical inference.'

Test sets are small (50 tasks per level, 10 eval), so tier-level accuracies and LRL differences between adjacent models carry substantial sampling noise that is not quantified (no confidence intervals or significance testing).

The training study is thin for its claims: only one model (Llama-3.1-8B) is tuned, only SFT (the RL/RLVR path is described but not evaluated), there is no ablation isolating the curriculum ordering (the paper notes training 'without shuffling' but never compares against shuffled-order or non-curriculum SFT), and comparisons of a fine-tuned on-distribution model against zero-shot closed models are somewhat apples-to-oranges.

Presentation defects: App. D ('Example: Task Synthesis Process') is effectively empty; Fig. 1 contains a typo ('Valdiation'); Tab. 1 has citation inconsistencies (e.g., Big-Bench row cites Phan et al. 2025), which suggests the comparison table needs more care.

Related-work positioning, while broad, does not deeply differentiate SLR from closely adjacent synthetic-ILP/verifiable-reasoning efforts (e.g., SynLogic, FLD, V-LoL, Logic-RL); the delta is mostly packaging (curriculum + symbolic judge) rather than a fundamentally new capability.
Code and data are 'to be released after publication,' so reproducibility currently rests on the manuscript description alone.

strengths: The core framework is technically sound: tasks are generated from an explicit language/configuration specification, ground-truth rules and executable validation programs are produced automatically, and evaluation is performed by a deterministic symbolic judge rather than an LLM judge or exact-match heuristics, which removes a major source of evaluation noise and subjectivity.

The paper delivers a complete artifact package: the SLR synthesis framework, a 19k-task 20-level curriculum (SLR-BENCH), a large leaderboard over conventional and reasoning LLMs (16 models), and a fine-tuned model with training details (LoRA, hyperparameters, hardware, evaluation harness) sufficient for reproduction once the promised code is released.

The synthesis algorithm (Alg. 1) is clearly specified, with principled control over rule length, background sampling, class balance, and curriculum tiering; the combinatorial size analysis in Tab. 2 supports the claimed difficulty gradient.

The empirical analysis yields interpretable findings: a sharp syntax-vs-semantic gap (high syntactic validity, low reasoning accuracy), performance collapse on medium/hard tiers, diminishing returns of test-time compute, and quantified cost escalation, which are genuinely useful community insights.

The related-work comparison (Tab. 1) is comprehensive and fairly positions SLR against existing synthetic logic benchmarks (K&K, ZebraLogic, FLD, KOR-Bench, etc.) along axes of custom tasks, curriculum, and scalable complexity.
The limitation and ethics sections are candid and appropriate; the synthetic nature of the benchmark legitimately mitigates contamination/memorization concerns.
weaknesses: The central 'curriculum learning' claim is not adequately supported by an ablation: the SFT training presents data sequentially without shuffling, but there is no control experiment with the same data shuffled or with only low/high levels. The reported gains (Tab. 3) could be attributable to SFT on synthetic logic data alone rather than to the curriculum ordering, which is the paper's headline contribution.

Only one base model (Llama-3.1-8B) is fine-tuned, and no RL experiments are reported despite the framework being motivated substantially by RLVR (Fig. 1, Sec. 3.3); generality of the training claims across models and training methods is therefore untested.

The per-level test sets are very small (50 test and 10 eval samples per level), so per-tier accuracy figures and the LRL metric have substantial sampling noise; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for any comparison, including the downstream benchmark deltas (some of which are small, e.g., +0.9 LogiQA).

The task domain is a single ILP family (single definite-clause east/westbound rules over a trains vocabulary, closely following V-LoL/Michalski trains), which narrows the scope of conclusions such as 'LLMs Can't Do Induction at Scale'; evidence is confined to one domain with one rule per task.

Some framing slightly overstates results: 'doubles accuracy' refers to the LRL metric (3.6 to 8.8), while hard-tier accuracy remains at 5%; the parity claim with Gemini-Flash-Thinking rests partly on models with missing compute information (footnoted 'information not available').

Reproducibility is contingent: code and data 'will be made publicly available after publication' rather than being verifiable at review time, and Appendix D is essentially empty (content deferred to a figure), with several writing/copy errors ('Valdiation', '(vi) Problem Size' where (iv) is meant) suggesting insufficient polish.

The strongest reasoning model (o3) solves only 45% of hard tasks and 74% of medium tasks, raising the possibility that some high-level tasks are underspecified or ambiguous rather than merely difficult; no error analysis or human-solvability validation of generated tasks is provided.

strengths: The core contribution is well-motivated and addresses a genuine gap: an automated, contamination-resistant pipeline for inductive (not just deductive) logical reasoning tasks with deterministic, executable verification (symbolic judge), avoiding the well-known pitfalls of LLM-as-judge and multiple-choice evaluation.

The SLR framework is cleanly specified (Alg. 1, formal definitions of OVERALLSCORE/PARTIALSCORE, language/configuration parameters), giving precise, controllable difficulty and extensibility — a reusable artifact beyond the specific benchmark.
SLR-BENCH itself is substantial: 19k tasks across 20 curriculum levels with documented combinatorial scaling, plus a useful worked example of synthesis (Fig. 6) that aids reproducibility.

The large-scale evaluation across ~15 conventional and reasoning LLMs yields credible, interesting findings: the syntax/semantics gap, diminishing returns of test-time compute (e.g., o3 vs. GPT-4o token/cost analysis), and marginal returns to parameter scaling.

Training and evaluation details are unusually thorough (hyperparameters, DeepSpeed/LoRA setup, evaluation harness, pricing tables, licenses, limitations and risk sections), and code/data release is promised.
Downstream generalization (MMLU subcategories, LogiQA, ARC, HellaSwag, GPQA) goes beyond in-domain gains and makes the contribution relevant to the broader NLP reasoning community.
weaknesses: The headline curriculum-learning claim lacks essential controls. The reported doubling of Llama-3-8B accuracy conflates (a) SFT on synthetic ILP data at all, (b) sequential curriculum ordering, and (c) the SLR reward machinery. A shuffled-difficulty SFT baseline or SFT on generic Prolog/rule-induction data is needed to attribute the gains to 'curriculum learning' specifically. As presented, any SFT on the benchmark's training split would likely produce large in-domain gains.

Reinforcement learning with the verifiable logic rewards is presented as a core feature of the framework (Fig. 1, abstract, Sec. 3.3), but no RL experiments are reported — only SFT. This leaves the framework's main training-side selling point empirically untested.

Statistical rigor is thin for the reported magnitudes: only 50 test tasks per level (10 eval), single pass@1 attempt, and no confidence intervals or significance tests for either the leaderboard comparisons or the downstream benchmark deltas (several of which, e.g., +0.9 on LogiQA, are well within typical eval noise).

Generalization claims are narrower than the abstract suggests: the tuned 8B model reaches LRL 8.8 versus o3's 15.5, and 'parity with Gemini-Flash-Thinking' rests on an 8.8 vs. 8.6 margin against a single, non-frontier reasoning model. The hard tier remains essentially unsolved (5%), so the extent of true inductive capability transfer is unclear.

Benchmark scope is narrow relative to the framing: one domain (trains, adapted from V-LoL), a single ground-truth rule per task, function-free definite clauses. Claims about 'inductive reasoning at scale' would be better supported by at least one additional domain instantiation demonstrating the framework's claimed extensibility.

Potential leakage within the pipeline is not fully addressed: 30% of rules at levels 6–20 are LLM-guided, so the rule distribution partially reflects an LLM's priors; and since the model is SFT'd on ground-truth rules from the same generator, in-domain test performance may partially reflect fitting the generator's stylistic distribution rather than general inductive reasoning. No analysis (e.g., performance on held-out rule types) is provided.

Several claims are phrased more strongly than the evidence (e.g., 'fully automated ... requires no human annotations' while LLM-guided rule generation introduces its own distributional biases; cost claims tied to a fixed pricing date and ignoring caching).
The code and dataset are promised only 'after publication,' so full reproducibility cannot be verified at review time.

strengths: SLR is a well-engineered, fully automated synthesis pipeline for inductive logical reasoning tasks with verifiable, deterministic symbolic rewards, addressing a genuine gap: most existing benchmarks target deduction and rely on exact-match or LLM-judge evaluation (Tab. 1 positioning is informative).

SLR-BENCH provides fine-grained, parameterized control over difficulty (rule length, problem size, background sampling, vocabulary), and the ablations (App. Tab. 7) convincingly demonstrate that synthesis parameters actually modulate task complexity rather than difficulty being arbitrary.

Large-scale evaluation spanning ~50 models including o3, GPT-5, o1, Qwen3, and Llama families, with token/cost accounting, yields reproducible and interesting findings: sharp accuracy collapse with complexity, limited gains from parameter scaling, diminishing returns from test-time compute, and the syntax-vs-semantics gap.

Training experiments go beyond a single model: SFT on Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen3-8B plus GRPO on DeepSeek-R1-1.5B, with zero-shot transfer to an OOD domain (SLR-Homes) and a broad set of downstream benchmarks, supporting the claim of domain-agnostic gains rather than dataset-specific heuristics.

The error-mode taxonomy (App. G), including quantitative analysis of reward-hacking shortcuts in GPT-5 models and degenerate reasoning in distilled models, is a genuinely useful contribution that the symbolic judge uniquely enables.
The paper is clearly written, the framework formalization (LFE/ILP notation, Algorithm 1, scoring metrics in App. B.4) is precise, and the supplementary material is unusually thorough.
weaknesses: The task domain is narrow: a single-rule, function-free definite-clause classification task in the Michalski trains domain. Despite the framework's claimed generality, SLR-BENCH itself instantiates only one domain and one target predicate, which limits how far conclusions about 'inductive reasoning at scale' generalize; multi-rule and multi-domain instantiations are deferred to future work.

Test sets are very small (50 tasks per level, ~1000 test tasks total per leaderboard run, and tier accuracies computed over even fewer tasks), so reported accuracies, especially on Hard tiers, carry substantial statistical uncertainty; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported.

The curriculum-order ablation (Tab. 8) shows negligible differences (LRL 6.01 vs. 5.99 vs. 5.93), yet the paper repeatedly claims 'curriculum order matters' and 'the ordered curriculum achieves the best results'; this headline claim is not supported by the evidence.

Some downstream generalization gains are modest and heterogeneous (MMLU +2.8, GPQA +1.1, LogiQA +0.9 for Llama; MMLU-Stats 0.0 gain for Qwen3), and no baseline (e.g., SFT on a non-logical task of matched size) is included, so it is hard to attribute gains specifically to SLR's logical structure rather than to any additional instruction tuning.

Reproducibility is currently incomplete: code and data are stated to be released 'after publication' rather than available at review time, and LLM-guided rule generation introduces an additional nondeterministic component whose rules cannot be regenerated exactly.
Cost comparisons between open-weight and API models conflate token counts and per-token pricing and ignore server-side caching; the '$300 per 1000 prompts' framing could be more carefully caveated.

The closed-world-assumption Prolog entailment setup and the restriction to semantic-equivalence-via-coverage may admit degenerate but 'correct' hypotheses (a point the authors partially acknowledge), and the paper does not measure how often judged-correct rules diverge meaningfully from the intended concept.

Minor overclaims and inconsistencies: the abstract asserts capabilities 'generalize to a wide range of established benchmarks' based partly on small deltas, and Tab. 2's framing ('surpasses baseline across all curriculum stages') glosses over Hard-tier performance near zero (5%).

strengths: Well-motivated problem: the paper targets inductive reasoning (rather than the more common deductive focus) and addresses benchmark contamination through fully synthetic task generation with symbolic, deterministic verification.

The SLR framework is cleanly specified (Alg. 1, LFE/ILP formalization, Herbrand-base sampling, mirror sampling), and the ablations (Tab. 7) demonstrate that synthesis parameters genuinely modulate difficulty, supporting the claim of controlled complexity.

Substantial empirical breadth: an extended leaderboard covering ~50 models (App. Tab. 16), test-time scaling and pass@k analyses, curriculum-order ablations, GRPO experiments, and a taxonomy of failure modes with quantitative support (App. G), including the interesting finding of reward-hacking/shortcut behavior in frontier reasoning models.

The paper is generally well-organized, and the symbolic-judge evaluation methodology (semantic correctness independent of surface form) is a sound design choice; limitations and licensing are discussed candidly.
weaknesses: Narrow task domain: all 19k tasks derive from a single Michalski-style trains domain with single-rule, function-free Horn clauses. The claimed generality ('scalable logical reasoning', domain-agnostic reasoning capabilities) is not well supported by one instantiation; SLR-Homes is a token OOD test within the same framework.

Headline claims are overstated or confounded. 'Parity with Gemini-Flash-Thinking at a fraction of the cost' compares a model fine-tuned on the same task distribution (levels 1–15 of SLR-BENCH) against a zero-shot reasoning model on the authors' own benchmark; this is an in-domain training advantage, not evidence of superior general reasoning. Similarly, downstream gains are small (MMLU +2.8, ARC +1.4, HellaSwag +1.5) and would plausibly arise from any instruction-tuning/LoRA procedure; no control fine-tuning baseline (e.g., generic SFT on non-reasoning data of similar budget) is reported.

Statistical rigor is insufficient. Test sets are only 50 tasks per level (1,000 test tasks total) and eval sets 10 tasks; no confidence intervals, variance estimates, or significance tests accompany the headline improvements (e.g., LRL 8.7 vs 3.8 is credible, but tier-level differences and downstream deltas of 1–3 points are not interpretable without uncertainty).

Reproducibility is asserted but not yet demonstrable: code and data 'will be made publicly available after publication', so none of the central artifacts (synthesizer, symbolic judge, benchmark splits, prompts) can currently be verified. Given that the entire contribution rests on automated synthesis correctness, this is a significant gap.

Potential biases in synthesis are underexplored: 30% of rules from level 6 onward are LLM-guided, yet the paper does not analyze whether LLM-generated rules are systematically easier/harder or distributed differently, and the data-leakage guarantees (App. B.6) acknowledge that semantic overlap cannot be ruled out.

Several results are presented inconsistently or without sufficient detail: Fig. 3 plots model performance without identifying which model; the curriculum-order ablation (Tab. 8) shows differences of ~0.1 LRL between ordered and random conditions yet concludes ordering 'matters'; the GRPO run was halted early by reward collapse, weakening the RL claim; the 'more green than yellow' example in App. B.5 (and duplicated rules 10/11) suggests insufficient quality control over LLM-guided rules.

Cost analyses rely on list prices and ignore caching (acknowledged), and the token/cost comparison conflates model price with reasoning effort, making cross-model efficiency claims (e.g., '730× less compute') more rhetorical than precise.

strengths: Well-motivated and clearly positioned contribution: SLR targets inductive (rather than deductive) logical reasoning with a fully automated, contamination-resistant synthesis pipeline and deterministic symbolic evaluation, filling a genuine gap relative to existing benchmarks (Tab. 1 comparison is informative).

The synthesis framework is technically sound: rule/background separation, stratified rejection sampling, mirror sampling, and controllable knobs (rule length, problem size, sampling policy) are well specified, and ablations (App. E.1) empirically demonstrate that these knobs modulate difficulty as intended.

Very broad empirical coverage: a large leaderboard of 50+ models spanning OpenAI, Gemini, DeepSeek, Qwen, and Llama families, with SFT (Llama, Qwen), GRPO (DeepSeek-R1-1.5B), curriculum-order ablations, pass@k/CoT analyses, and a qualitative error-mode taxonomy (reward-hacking shortcuts in GPT-5, degenerate loops in distilled models) that is genuinely interesting.

Evidence of transfer beyond the synthetic domain (CLUTRR with large compute savings, MMLU-Stats +17) supports the claim that SLR training induces generalizable inductive biases rather than dataset-specific heuristics.
Honest limitations section, detailed training/evaluation hyperparameters, and transparent cost accounting make the work largely followable and reproducible in principle.
weaknesses: Narrow task domain: all SLR-BENCH tasks derive from a single Michalski-style trains domain with single-rule, function-free definite clauses and highly templated prompts. The headline claim 'LLMs Can't Do Induction at Scale' is stronger than the evidence; results may partly reflect Prolog-style pattern completion or template familiarity rather than general inductive reasoning.

Thin statistical support for key claims: test sets are only 50 tasks per level, single-run experiments, no variance estimates, seeds, or significance tests. The claim of 'parity with Gemini-Flash-Thinking' rests on LRL 8.7 vs 8.6, an in-domain comparison for a model trained on SLR tasks, which is a weak basis for the 'outperforms reasoning LLMs' framing in the abstract and intro.

Downstream transfer evidence is mixed: many downstream deltas are small (+0.9 to +2.8 on LogiQA, GPQA, ARC, HellaSwag) and could fall within run-to-run noise; only CLUTRR and MMLU-Stats show large gains. Selective emphasis on positives without uncertainty quantification weakens the generalization narrative.

Code and data are 'made publicly available after publication', so reproducibility cannot be verified at review time; several appendix items show signs of insufficient checking (duplicated rule examples in App. B.5 items 10 and 11, apparent inconsistency in the Fig. 2 validation example, typos such as 'Valdiation', malformed references like 'et.al., 2025', duplicate Gao et al. entries).

Novelty is incremental: synthetic verifiable-reasoning benchmarks (FLD, SynLogic, PrOntoQA, K&K, Logic-RL) already exist; the Tab. 1 self-comparison overstates uniqueness, and the main advance is the curriculum organization plus integration rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.
Some analysis is post-hoc and interpretive (e.g., attributing GPT-5 shortcut behavior to RL training objectives) without controlled experiments to support the causal explanation.
